ateAvocado.steps[0].title: Step 1: Determine What Was Ingested
ateAvocado.steps[0].content: Check if the pit was swallowed. The flesh alone causes mild GI upset, but the pit is a life-threatening obstruction hazard.
ateAvocado.steps[1].title: Step 2: Do NOT Induce Vomiting If Pit Was Swallowed
ateAvocado.steps[1].content: ⚠️ If your dog ate the pit, do NOT induce vomiting — it can lodge in the esophagus on the way back up, causing worse obstruction.
ateAvocado.steps[2].title: Step 3: Watch for Guacamole Ingredients
ateAvocado.steps[2].content: If your dog ate guacamole, check the ingredients — onion, garlic, lime, and salt are additional toxins. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435.
ateAvocado.steps[3].title: Step 4: Monitor for Symptoms
ateAvocado.steps[3].content: Watch for vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, difficulty defecating (sign of obstruction), and lethargy. Symptoms usually appear within 2-12 hours.
ateAvocado.timeline[0].description: Mild GI signs from flesh: vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain
ateAvocado.timeline[1].description: Obstruction signs from pit: vomiting, straining to defecate, abdominal pain, lethargy
ateAvocado.timeline[2].description: Risk window: untreated obstruction can progress to intestinal perforation or necrosis
ateAvocado.faqs[0].question: Are avocados toxic to dogs?
ateAvocado.faqs[0].answer: Avocado contains persin, a fungicidal toxin that is mildly toxic to dogs. The flesh causes mild GI upset in most dogs, but the pit (seed) poses a far greater danger as it can cause life-threatening intestinal obstruction. The skin and leaves also contain higher persin concentrations than the flesh.
ateAvocado.faqs[1].question: What should I do if my dog ate an avocado pit?
ateAvocado.faqs[1].answer: If your dog swallowed an avocado pit, contact your vet immediately. The pit is large enough to cause intestinal blockage, especially in small and medium dogs. Do NOT induce vomiting — the pit can lodge in the esophagus on the way back up. Your vet will X-ray to locate the pit and determine if surgical removal is needed.
ateAvocado.faqs[2].question: How much avocado is dangerous for dogs?
ateAvocado.faqs[2].answer: The flesh has low toxicity — most dogs experience only mild vomiting or diarrhea from eating avocado flesh. However, the pit is a choking hazard and obstruction risk regardless of amount. The leaves and skin contain higher persin levels and should be avoided. Pancreatitis risk increases with large amounts due to high fat content.
ateAvocado.faqs[3].question: Can dogs eat guacamole?
ateAvocado.faqs[3].answer: No, guacamole is especially dangerous for dogs because it typically contains onion, garlic, lime juice, and salt — all of which are toxic to dogs. Onion and garlic cause hemolytic anemia, salt can cause ion poisoning, and lime peel contains essential oils. Call your vet immediately if your dog ate guacamole.

ateCaffeine.riskAssessment.rows[0].actio: 🚨 Emergency vet NOW for small dogs
ateCaffeine.riskAssessment.rows[1].actio: 📞 Call vet or poison control immediately
ateCaffeine.steps[0].title: Step 1: Act Fast — Caffeine Absorbs Quickly
ateCaffeine.steps[0].content: Remove any remaining caffeine source. Caffeine is absorbed within 30-60 minutes — time is critical for decontamination.
ateCaffeine.steps[1].title: Step 2: Call Poison Control or Vet Immediately
ateCaffeine.steps[1].content: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Have the product label ready to report caffeine content in mg.
ateCaffeine.steps[2].title: Step 3: Do NOT Induce Vomiting If Symptoms Present
ateCaffeine.steps[2].content: ⚠️ If your dog shows trembling, hyperactivity, or seizures, inducing vomiting risks aspiration. Only induce if instructed by a professional AND your dog is asymptomatic within 30 minutes of ingestion.
ateCaffeine.steps[3].title: Step 4: Monitor Heart and Breathing
ateCaffeine.steps[3].content: Watch for rapid breathing, restlessness, and elevated heart rate. Caffeine causes cardiac arrhythmias — if your dog collapses or has difficulty breathing, go to emergency vet NOW.
ateCaffeine.timeline[0].description: Early signs: restlessness, hyperactivity, vomiting, elevated heart rate
ateCaffeine.timeline[1].description: Severe signs: tremors, seizures, cardiac arrhythmias, collapse
ateCaffeine.timeline[2].description: Resolution with treatment: hospitalization typically required 24-48 hours; good prognosis with early care
ateCaffeine.faqs[0].question: How much caffeine is toxic to dogs?
ateCaffeine.faqs[0].answer: Mild symptoms appear at 20mg/kg of body weight. Severe toxicity occurs at 60mg/kg. The lethal dose (LD50) is approximately 140mg/kg. For a 20kg dog, this equals roughly 2,800mg of caffeine — about 28 cups of coffee. However, even small amounts (1-2 caffeine pills of 200mg each) can cause serious symptoms in small dogs.
ateCaffeine.faqs[1].question: What are the symptoms of caffeine poisoning in dogs?
ateCaffeine.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms appear within 1-2 hours and include: restlessness, hyperactivity, vomiting, elevated heart rate, tremors, seizures, and collapse. Caffeine is absorbed rapidly and affects the central nervous system and cardiovascular system. Severe cases cause cardiac arrhythmias that can be fatal.
ateCaffeine.faqs[2].question: Should I induce vomiting if my dog ate caffeine?
ateCaffeine.faqs[2].answer: Inducing vomiting may be recommended if ingestion occurred within 30 minutes and your dog is alert. However, caffeine is rapidly absorbed and can cause seizures — never induce vomiting if your dog shows any neurological symptoms. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 for guidance.
ateCaffeine.faqs[3].question: What is the treatment for caffeine poisoning in dogs?
ateCaffeine.faqs[3].answer: Treatment includes: induced vomiting (if early), activated charcoal to reduce absorption, IV fluids for elimination, anti-arrhythmic medications for heart issues, anti-seizure medications, and temperature regulation. Hospitalization is typically required for 24-48 hours. Prognosis is good with early treatment.

ateAlcohol.steps[0].title: Step 1: Remove All Alcohol Immediately
ateAlcohol.steps[0].content: Take away any remaining beverages, food containing alcohol, or raw bread dough. Clean up any spills — dogs may lick floors.
ateAlcohol.steps[1].title: Step 2: Assess Your Dog's Neurological State
ateAlcohol.steps[1].content: Check: Can your dog walk normally? Are they alert or depressed? Vomiting? If your dog cannot stand or is unconscious — go to emergency vet NOW.
ateAlcohol.steps[2].title: Step 3: Call Poison Control
ateAlcohol.steps[2].content: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Calculate approximate alcohol consumed in grams: volume (mL) × alcohol% × 0.789 = grams of ethanol.
ateAlcohol.steps[3].title: Step 4: Keep Your Dog Safe
ateAlcohol.steps[3].content: Prevent falls due to ataxia. Keep your dog warm — alcohol causes vasodilation and hypothermia. Do NOT leave them unattended. Monitor breathing and consciousness every 15 minutes.
ateAlcohol.timeline[0].description: Early signs: disorientation, ataxia (wobbly gait), vomiting, depression
ateAlcohol.timeline[1].description: Severe signs: slowed breathing, metabolic acidosis, hypothermia, hypoglycemia (especially small dogs/puppies)
ateAlcohol.timeline[2].description: Resolution with supportive care: IV fluids, glucose, blood pH monitoring; unmonitored cases risk coma or death
ateAlcohol.faqs[0].question: Is alcohol toxic to dogs?
ateAlcohol.faqs[0].answer: Yes, alcohol (ethanol) is highly toxic to dogs. The lethal dose is 5.5 mL/kg of pure ethanol. Dogs are much more sensitive than humans because they lack efficient alcohol dehydrogenase enzymes. Even small amounts cause ataxia, depression, and metabolic acidosis. Beer, wine, liquor, and raw bread dough all pose serious risks.
ateAlcohol.faqs[1].question: What are the symptoms of alcohol poisoning in dogs?
ateAlcohol.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms appear within 30-90 minutes: disorientation, loss of coordination (ataxia), vomiting, depression, slowed breathing, metabolic acidosis, and in severe cases, coma and death. Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) is a dangerous complication, especially in small dogs and puppies.
ateAlcohol.faqs[2].question: Can beer kill a dog?
ateAlcohol.faqs[2].answer: Yes, beer can kill a dog. A single 12oz beer (5% alcohol = 17g ethanol) can cause severe intoxication in a small dog (under 10kg). Dogs metabolize alcohol much slower than humans, so effects accumulate. Carbonation also speeds absorption. Never intentionally give alcohol to dogs.
ateAlcohol.faqs[3].question: What should I do if my dog accidentally drank alcohol?
ateAlcohol.faqs[3].answer: Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 or your vet immediately. Do NOT induce vomiting if your dog shows neurological symptoms (depression, ataxia). Remove any remaining alcohol. Keep your dog warm and safe from falls. Your vet may need to administer IV fluids, glucose, and monitor blood pH.

ateAlcohol.vetDecision.emergency[1]: Severe ataxia with inability to stand
ateAlcohol.vetDecision.urgent[2]: Known ingestion of raw bread dough
ateAlcohol.vetDecision.monitor[2]: Alert and walking normally after 1 hour

ateMacadamiaNuts.steps[0].title: Step 1: Don't Panic, But Act Quickly
ateMacadamiaNuts.steps[0].content: Remove any remaining macadamia nuts from your dog's reach. Stay calm — your dog will pick up on your stress.
ateMacadamiaNuts.steps[1].title: Step 2: Do NOT Induce Vomiting (Unless Instructed)
ateMacadamiaNuts.steps[1].content: ⚠️ Inducing vomiting can cause aspiration pneumonia. Only induce vomiting if explicitly instructed by a veterinarian or poison control.
ateMacadamiaNuts.steps[2].title: Step 3: Gather Critical Information
ateMacadamiaNuts.steps[3].title: Step 4: Contact Professional Help
ateMacadamiaNuts.timeline[0].description: Early signs: weakness in hind legs, ataxia (wobbly gait), vomiting
ateMacadamiaNuts.timeline[1].description: Progression: tremors, reluctance to stand, abdominal pain, elevated temperature (up to 104°F/40°C)
ateMacadamiaNuts.timeline[2].description: Resolution: symptoms typically resolve with supportive care; full recovery expected
ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs[0].question: Are macadamia nuts toxic to dogs?
ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs[0].answer: Yes, macadamia nuts are uniquely toxic to dogs. The exact toxin is unknown, but even small amounts cause weakness in hind legs, vomiting, tremors, and hyperthermia. The minimum toxic dose is approximately 2.4 g/kg of body weight. Most dogs recover within 48 hours with supportive veterinary care.
ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs[1].question: How many macadamia nuts are dangerous for a dog?
ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs[1].answer: For a 20kg (44lb) dog, as few as 10-12 nuts can cause symptoms. Smaller dogs may react to just 2-3 nuts. The toxic threshold is approximately 0.5g of nuts per kg of body weight for mild symptoms, with severe symptoms appearing at 2.4g/kg.
ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs[2].question: How long after eating macadamia nuts will my dog show symptoms?
ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs[2].answer: Symptoms typically appear within 3-12 hours after ingestion. The earliest sign is usually weakness or paralysis of the hind legs, followed by vomiting, tremors, abdominal pain, and elevated body temperature (up to 104°F/40°C).
ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs[3].question: Can a dog die from eating macadamia nuts?
ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs[3].answer: Fatalities from macadamia nut poisoning are extremely rare. The LD50 is 2.4g/kg, meaning a 20kg dog would need to eat approximately 48g of nuts (about 40-50 nuts) to reach dangerous levels. However, even sub-lethal doses cause significant discomfort and require veterinary monitoring.
ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs[4].question: Should I induce vomiting if my dog ate macadamia nuts?
ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs[4].answer: Do NOT induce vomiting unless instructed by a veterinarian. Induction is only effective within 30 minutes of ingestion and can cause aspiration pneumonia. Contact ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 for specific guidance based on the amount consumed and time elapsed.

ateMushrooms.riskAssessment.rows[0].acti: 🚨 Emergency vet NOW — do not wait
ateMushrooms.steps[0].title: THIS IS A TRUE EMERGENCY
ateMushrooms.steps[0].content: Do NOT wait for symptoms. Amatoxin poisoning has a deceptive delay — your dog looks fine for 6-24 hours while the toxin destroys the liver. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 NOW.
ateMushrooms.steps[1].title: Collect a Mushroom Sample
ateMushrooms.steps[1].content: If safe, collect remaining mushroom pieces (including base/bulb). Place in a paper bag (not plastic). This helps mycologists identify the species and determine toxicity risk.
ateMushrooms.steps[2].title: Go to Emergency Vet for Decontamination
ateMushrooms.steps[2].content: Your vet will induce vomiting (if within 2 hours), administer activated charcoal, and start IV fluids. They will monitor liver enzymes for 48-72 hours. Early treatment is the ONLY effective defense.
ateMushrooms.steps[3].title: Prepare for Hospitalization
ateMushrooms.steps[3].content: If amatoxin poisoning is confirmed, treatment includes: Penicillin G, Silymarin (milk thistle), N-acetylcysteine, IV fluids, and potentially plasma transfusions. Hospitalization typically lasts 3-7 days.
ateMushrooms.timeline[0].description: Latent phase: dog appears normal. Toxin is being absorbed.
ateMushrooms.timeline[1].description: Gastroenteritis phase: explosive vomiting and diarrhea begin. This is the BEST treatment window.
ateMushrooms.timeline[2].description: False recovery: symptoms temporarily improve. Owners think dog is healing — FALSE sense of security.
ateMushrooms.timeline[3].description: Fulminant liver failure: jaundice, bleeding disorders, hepatic encephalopathy, death without aggressive treatment.
ateMushrooms.faqs[0].question: Are wild mushrooms toxic to dogs?
ateMushrooms.faqs[0].answer: Many wild mushroom species are extremely toxic to dogs. The most dangerous is Amanita phalloides (Death Cap), which contains amatoxins that cause irreversible liver failure. Other toxic genera include Galerina, Lepiota, and Cortinarius. Even non-lethal species can cause severe GI upset. ANY mushroom ingestion should be treated as an emergency because you cannot reliably identify species in the field.
ateMushrooms.faqs[1].question: How long after eating a mushroom will my dog show symptoms?
ateMushrooms.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms from amatoxin-containing mushrooms (Amanita) are DELAYED 6-24 hours. A dog appears fine initially, then develops explosive vomiting and diarrhea. After a brief "false recovery" of 12-24 hours, liver failure begins. By the time jaundice appears, damage is often irreversible. Other species cause symptoms within 30 minutes to 6 hours.
ateMushrooms.faqs[2].question: What should I do if my dog ate a wild mushroom?
ateMushrooms.faqs[2].answer: Treat EVERY wild mushroom ingestion as a life-threatening emergency. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 immediately. Your vet will induce vomiting (if within 2 hours), administer activated charcoal, and admit for 48-72 hour observation with liver enzyme monitoring. Do NOT wait for symptoms — early treatment is the only effective defense against amatoxin poisoning.
ateMushrooms.faqs[3].question: Can a dog die from eating a mushroom?
ateMushrooms.faqs[3].answer: Yes. Amanita phalloides (Death Cap) has a 50-100% mortality rate in dogs without treatment. Amatoxins destroy liver cells by inhibiting RNA polymerase II. Even with treatment, mortality remains 20-30%. The lethal dose is 0.1mg/kg of amatoxin — a single Death Cap cap contains 10-15mg. Early aggressive treatment (within 12 hours) significantly improves survival.
ateMushrooms.faqs[4].question: Can dogs eat store-bought mushrooms?
ateMushrooms.faqs[4].answer: Store-bought mushrooms (white button, cremini, portobello) are generally safe for dogs in small amounts. However, they offer little nutritional value and can cause GI upset if fed in large quantities or cooked with butter/oil/garlic. Never assume a field mushroom is safe — only eat mushrooms you purchased from a grocery store.

ateCookedBones.riskAssessment.rows[1].ac: 🚨 Vet within 1 hour — hollow bones splinter
ateCookedBones.steps[0].title: Do NOT Induce Vomiting
ateCookedBones.steps[0].content: ⚠️ This is critical: vomiting can cause sharp bone fragments to lodge in the esophagus or puncture tissue on the way back up.
ateCookedBones.steps[1].title: Offer Soft Food to Cushion Fragments
ateCookedBones.steps[1].content: Feed bread, cooked rice, or canned pumpkin to help cushion small bone fragments and reduce injury risk. This does NOT replace veterinary evaluation.
ateCookedBones.steps[2].title: Call Your Vet for X-Ray Assessment
ateCookedBones.steps[2].content: Your vet will X-ray to locate bone fragments, assess obstruction risk, and determine if endoscopic or surgical removal is needed.
ateCookedBones.steps[3].title: Monitor Stool for 3 Days
ateCookedBones.steps[3].content: Watch for: bone fragments in stool (normal passage), black/tarry stool (GI bleeding), inability to defecate (obstruction), or blood. Report any abnormalities to your vet immediately.
ateCookedBones.timeline[0].description: Critical window: vet can induce vomiting (if advised) or perform endoscopy. Do NOT induce without professional guidance.
ateCookedBones.timeline[1].description: Fragments may cause esophageal or stomach perforation. Symptoms: drooling, reluctance to eat, pawing at mouth, vomiting.
ateCookedBones.timeline[2].description: Intestinal obstruction or perforation symptoms appear: vomiting, no bowel movement, abdominal pain, black tarry stool.
ateCookedBones.timeline[3].description: If bones passed without complications, no further action needed. If surgery was performed, recovery period.
ateCookedBones.faqs[0].question: Why are cooked bones dangerous for dogs?
ateCookedBones.faqs[0].answer: Cooked bones become brittle and splinter into sharp fragments. These shards can: (1) puncture the esophagus, stomach, or intestinal wall, (2) cause life-threatening peritonitis, (3) create intestinal obstruction, or (4) become lodged in the jaw or throat. Raw bones are safer because they are more flexible, but cooked bones are NEVER safe.
ateCookedBones.faqs[1].question: What are the symptoms if my dog ate cooked bones?
ateCookedBones.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms of bone-related injury include: vomiting (possibly bloody), diarrhea (may contain blood or look black/tarry), abdominal pain (hunched posture, reluctance to move), difficulty defecating, excessive drooling, pawing at mouth, and lethargy. Symptoms may appear within hours or be delayed 1-3 days if a slow obstruction develops.
ateCookedBones.faqs[2].question: Should I induce vomiting if my dog ate cooked bones?
ateCookedBones.faqs[2].answer: Do NOT induce vomiting if your dog ate cooked bones. Regurgitating sharp bone fragments can cause additional damage to the esophagus or become lodged in the throat. Contact your vet or ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 for immediate guidance.
ateCookedBones.faqs[3].question: What is the treatment for bone ingestion in dogs?
ateCookedBones.faqs[3].answer: Treatment depends on severity: (1) If bone is lodged in throat/mouth — manual removal under sedation. (2) If bone is in stomach — endoscopic retrieval. (3) If obstruction or perforation — emergency surgery. (4) If small, softened pieces — monitoring with bread/bulk diet to cushion passage. X-rays or ultrasound determine the approach.

atePlastic.steps[0].title: Assess the Ingested Object
atePlastic.steps[0].content: If possible, find the remaining pieces and measure them. Was it a wrapper, toy piece, or bag? Size and shape determine risk.
atePlastic.steps[1].title: Do NOT Induce Vomiting If Large or Sharp
atePlastic.steps[1].content: ⚠️ Large objects can lodge in the esophagus; sharp edges can cause damage during regurgitation. Only induce if instructed by a vet for small, smooth items within 30 minutes of ingestion.
atePlastic.steps[2].title: Feed a Bulk Meal
atePlastic.steps[2].content: Offer bread, canned pumpkin, or cooked rice to help wrap the plastic and encourage safe passage. This is NOT a substitute for veterinary care if the object is large.
atePlastic.steps[3].title: Monitor Closely for 48 Hours
atePlastic.steps[3].content: Check: Is your dog eating? Vomiting? Defecating? Locate the plastic in stool if possible. Absence of bowel movement for 24+ hours with vomiting = emergency.
atePlastic.timeline[0].description: Assess the object. If small (<2cm), monitor. If large or sharp, call vet immediately.
atePlastic.timeline[1].description: Small pieces may pass through stomach. Watch for vomiting, lethargy, or abdominal pain.
atePlastic.timeline[2].description: Critical monitoring window. If no bowel movement AND vomiting = possible obstruction. Seek emergency care.
atePlastic.timeline[3].description: If still no bowel movement, X-ray needed to locate blockage. Surgery may be required if object is lodged.
atePlastic.faqs[0].question: Is plastic dangerous for dogs?
atePlastic.faqs[0].answer: Plastic is non-toxic but can cause life-threatening intestinal obstruction. The danger depends on the size and shape of the plastic object relative to your dog. Items larger than 2cm wide are unlikely to pass through the pylorus (stomach exit) or ileocecal junction. Sharp plastic edges can also cause GI perforation.
atePlastic.faqs[1].question: Symptoms of plastic blockage in dogs?
atePlastic.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms appear within 2-48 hours: repeated vomiting (especially after eating), loss of appetite, lethargy, abdominal pain, absence of bowel movements, and dehydration. A complete obstruction causes persistent vomiting, dehydration, and shock within 24-72 hours. This is a surgical emergency.
atePlastic.faqs[2].question: How long does it take for plastic to pass through a dog?
atePlastic.faqs[2].answer: Small plastic pieces (under 2cm) typically pass through the GI tract within 24-48 hours and appear in stool. Larger items may take 3-5 days or become lodged. If plastic has not passed within 48 hours, or if vomiting occurs, veterinary intervention is required.
atePlastic.faqs[3].question: When should I call the vet if my dog ate plastic?
atePlastic.faqs[3].answer: Call your vet immediately if: (1) the plastic object is larger than 2cm in any dimension, (2) your dog vomits more than once, (3) no bowel movement occurs within 48 hours, (4) your dog shows abdominal pain or lethargy, or (5) the plastic piece is sharp/rigid. Do NOT wait for symptoms if the object is large.

ateMedication.riskAssessment.rows[0].act: 🚨 Emergency vet NOW — GI ulcers, kidney failure
ateMedication.steps[0].title: Gather All Medication Information
ateMedication.steps[0].content: Bring the pill bottle: drug name, strength (mg), number of pills missing. Calculate total mg consumed: strength × pills. This is critical for toxicity assessment.
ateMedication.steps[1].title: Call Poison Control IMMEDIATELY
ateMedication.steps[1].content: ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Do NOT wait for symptoms — some medications cause delayed toxicity.
ateMedication.steps[2].title: Do NOT Induce Vomiting Without Professional Guidance
ateMedication.steps[2].content: Some medications are rapidly absorbed; others can cause seizures if vomited. Only induce if ASPCA or your vet instructs you to.
ateMedication.steps[3].title: Go to Emergency Vet for Decontamination
ateMedication.steps[3].content: Your vet will induce vomiting (if early), administer activated charcoal, and begin IV fluids. Blood work will monitor liver/kidney function for 24-72 hours.
ateMedication.timeline[0].description: Best window for induced vomiting. Call poison control before inducing.
ateMedication.timeline[1].description: Drug absorption phase. Symptoms begin for fast-acting drugs (ibuprofen): vomiting, abdominal pain.
ateMedication.timeline[2].description: GI ulceration phase (NSAIDs). Symptoms: bloody vomiting, black tarry stool, kidney stress begins.
ateMedication.timeline[3].description: Organ damage phase: liver failure (acetaminophen), kidney failure (NSAIDs), seizures (antidepressants). Hospitalization required.
ateMedication.faqs[0].question: Which human medications are most toxic to dogs?
ateMedication.faqs[0].answer: The most dangerous human medications for dogs include: (1) NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) — GI ulcers and kidney failure at 50mg/kg. (2) Acetaminophen (Tylenol) — liver damage and methemoglobinemia at 75mg/kg. (3) Antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs) — serotonin syndrome. (4) ADHD medications (amphetamines) — severe stimulation. (5) Benzodiazepines — paradoxical agitation. (6) Vitamin D supplements — fatal hypercalcemia.
ateMedication.faqs[1].question: What are the symptoms of ibuprofen poisoning in dogs?
ateMedication.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms appear within 1-4 hours: vomiting (possibly with blood), loss of appetite, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. At toxic doses (50mg/kg+): kidney failure (increased thirst/urination, then decreased urine), GI ulceration, liver damage, and seizures. Megaesophagus (enlarged esophagus) can occur with chronic exposure. Treatment includes activated charcoal, gastroprotectants, IV fluids, and blood monitoring.
ateMedication.faqs[2].question: Should I induce vomiting if my dog ate medication?
ateMedication.faqs[2].answer: Inducing vomiting may be recommended if ingestion occurred within 30 minutes and your dog is alert. However, do NOT induce vomiting for: caustic substances, if your dog is already symptomatic (seizures, ataxia), or if the medication is rapidly absorbed. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 with the drug name, strength, and estimated number of pills consumed.
ateMedication.faqs[3].question: How is medication toxicity treated in dogs?
ateMedication.faqs[3].answer: Treatment depends on the drug: (1) Induced vomiting + activated charcoal (if early), (2) IV fluids for elimination, (3) Gastroprotectants (omeprazole, sucralfate) for NSAIDs, (4) N-acetylcysteine for acetaminophen, (5) Cyproheptadine for serotonin syndrome, (6) Lipid emulsion therapy for fat-soluble drugs. Hospitalization for 24-72 hours is typical for significant ingestions.

ateRodenticide.riskAssessment.rows[1].ac: 🚨 Emergency vet NOW — seizures within hours
ateRodenticide.steps[0].title: Step 1: This Is a Dire Emergency
ateRodenticide.steps[0].content: Do NOT wait for symptoms. Anticoagulant rodenticides have a 2-5 day delay before bleeding begins. By the time symptoms appear, the damage is done. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 NOW.
ateRodenticide.steps[1].title: Step 2: Bring the Product Package
ateRodenticide.steps[1].content: Take the bait package or a photo to the vet. The active ingredient determines treatment: anticoagulants need Vitamin K1; bromethalin needs brain swelling management; cholecalciferol needs calcium-lowering therapy.
ateRodenticide.steps[2].title: Step 3: Go to Emergency Vet for Decontamination
ateRodenticide.steps[2].content: Your vet will induce vomiting (if within 1-2 hours), administer activated charcoal, and start specific antidotes. For anticoagulants: Vitamin K1 for 4-6 weeks with blood clotting tests.
ateRodenticide.steps[3].title: Step 4: Hospitalization May Be Required
ateRodenticide.steps[3].content: Bromethalin poisoning requires 24-72 hour monitoring with mannitol for brain swelling. Anticoagulant cases need plasma transfusions if bleeding is active. Early treatment dramatically improves survival.
ateRodenticide.faqs[0].question: Is rat poison deadly to dogs?
ateRodenticide.faqs[0].answer: Yes, rat poison (rodenticide) is one of the most deadly toxins for dogs. There are two main types: (1) Anticoagulant rodenticides (warfarin, bromadiolone, brodifacoum) — prevent blood clotting, causing fatal internal bleeding. Single-dose types require one feeding; multiple-dose types are cumulative. (2) Neurotoxic rodenticides (bromethalin, strychnine, cholecalciferol) — cause brain swelling, seizures, or hypercalcium within hours. Without treatment, mortality rates are 50-90%.
ateRodenticide.faqs[1].question: What are the symptoms of rat poison in dogs?
ateRodenticide.faqs[1].answer: Anticoagulant symptoms appear 2-5 days after ingestion: weakness, pale gums, coughing blood, bloody vomit/diarrhea, nosebleeds, and collapse. Neurotoxic (bromethalin) symptoms appear within 2-24 hours: severe muscle tremors, seizures, ataxia, and paralysis. Cholecalciferol causes kidney failure with increased thirst/urination within 12-36 hours.
ateRodenticide.faqs[2].question: Can my dog survive rat poison?
ateRodenticide.faqs[2].answer: Yes, with immediate treatment. Anticoagulant poisoning is treatable with Vitamin K1 for 4-6 weeks; survival rate is 80-90% if treated before symptoms appear. Bromethalin has no antidote — treatment is supportive care (activated charcoal, mannitol for brain swelling) with 50-70% survival if treated early. Strychnine and cholecalciferol also require immediate veterinary intervention.
ateRodenticide.faqs[3].question: What should I do if my dog ate rat poison?
ateRodenticide.faqs[3].answer: Treat this as a dire emergency: (1) Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 immediately. (2) Go to the nearest emergency vet NOW — do not wait for symptoms. (3) Bring the product label to identify the active ingredient. (4) Induced vomiting within 1-2 hours may help prevent absorption. (5) Even if your dog seems fine, delayed symptoms are common and early treatment is life-saving.

ateTobacco.steps[0].title: Step 1: Calculate Total Nicotine
ateTobacco.steps[0].content: Count cigarettes/packages consumed. Cigarette: 10-15mg each. E-liquid: check mg/mL concentration × mL consumed. This determines toxicity risk.
ateTobacco.steps[1].title: Step 2: Call Poison Control IMMEDIATELY
ateTobacco.steps[1].content: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Nicotine is absorbed rapidly through oral mucosa — effects can begin within 15 minutes.
ateTobacco.steps[2].title: Step 3: Do NOT Induce Vomiting If Symptomatic
ateTobacco.steps[2].content: ⚠️ If your dog shows tremors, seizures, or agitation, inducing vomiting risks aspiration. Only induce if instructed by a professional AND your dog is asymptomatic within 15 minutes.
ateTobacco.steps[3].title: Step 4: Go to Emergency Vet for Monitoring
ateTobacco.steps[3].content: Your vet will administer activated charcoal, provide IV fluids, and monitor heart rhythm and respiratory function. Symptoms can progress rapidly.
ateTobacco.faqs[0].question: How much nicotine is toxic to dogs?
ateTobacco.faqs[0].answer: The toxic dose of nicotine in dogs is 20-100mg/kg. For a 20kg dog, this equals 400-2000mg of nicotine. Sources: 1 cigarette = 10-15mg nicotine, 1 cigarette butt = 5-7mg, nicotine patch = 8-21mg, nicotine gum = 2-4mg, e-liquid = 3-24mg/mL (highly concentrated). Even ONE cigarette can cause symptoms in a small dog.
ateTobacco.faqs[1].question: What are the symptoms of nicotine poisoning in dogs?
ateTobacco.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms appear within 15-60 minutes: hypersalivation, vomiting, tachycardia (rapid heart rate), muscle tremors, agitation, and hypertension. As toxicity progresses: bradycardia (slow heart rate), weakness, collapse, respiratory paralysis, and seizures. The biphasic effect — first excitation then depression — is characteristic of nicotine poisoning.
ateTobacco.faqs[2].question: Is vape liquid dangerous for dogs?
ateTobacco.faqs[2].answer: Yes, e-liquid (vape juice) is EXTREMELY dangerous due to high nicotine concentration. A single 10mL bottle can contain 30-240mg of nicotine — enough to kill multiple small dogs. The sweet flavorings also attract dogs. Ingestion of even small amounts requires emergency veterinary treatment.
ateTobacco.faqs[3].question: What should I do if my dog ate tobacco?
ateTobacco.faqs[3].answer: Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 immediately. Calculate total nicotine consumed: mg per item × number of items. Go to emergency vet if your dog ingested: (1) more than 1 cigarette, (2) any e-liquid, (3) a nicotine patch, or (4) any amount if your dog shows symptoms. Do NOT induce vomiting if seizures or tremors are present.

ateMarijuana.riskAssessment.rows[0].acti: 🚨 Emergency vet NOW — high THC + chocolate
ateMarijuana.riskAssessment.rows[2].acti: 📞 May also contain xylitol — call vet
ateMarijuana.steps[0].title: Step 1: Remove All Remaining Product
ateMarijuana.steps[0].content: Check for packaging — note THC content in mg per piece and total pieces eaten. This determines toxicity risk.
ateMarijuana.steps[1].title: Step 2: Check for Xylitol (CBD Products)
ateMarijuana.steps[1].content: ⚠️ Some CBD oils contain xylitol, which is extremely toxic to dogs. Check the ingredient list immediately.
ateMarijuana.steps[2].title: Step 3: Call Poison Control or Vet
ateMarijuana.steps[2].content: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Be honest — they will provide guidance without judgment.
ateMarijuana.steps[3].title: Step 4: Monitor Symptoms
ateMarijuana.steps[3].content: Watch for: stumbling, dilated pupils, urinary incontinence, drooling, slow heart rate, hypothermia. Severe cases: seizures or coma. Symptoms can last 12-72 hours.
ateMarijuana.faqs[0].question: Is marijuana toxic to dogs?
ateMarijuana.faqs[0].answer: Yes, THC (tetrahydrocannabinol) is toxic to dogs. Dogs have more cannabinoid receptors (CB1) in the brain than humans, making them significantly more sensitive. Edibles (gummies, brownies, cookies) are especially dangerous due to high THC concentration — one gummy can contain 10-100mg THC, which is toxic to most dogs.
ateMarijuana.faqs[1].question: What are the symptoms of marijuana poisoning in dogs?
ateMarijuana.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms appear within 30-90 minutes: dazed appearance, stumbling/ataxia, urinary incontinence (dripping urine), drooling, dilated pupils, vomiting, tremors, bradycardia (slow heart rate), hypothermia, and in severe cases: seizures or coma. Be honest with your vet — marijuana toxicosis is rarely fatal, and honesty ensures proper treatment.
ateMarijuana.faqs[2].question: Are marijuana edibles more dangerous than dried cannabis?
ateMarijuana.faqs[2].answer: Yes, edibles are significantly more dangerous: (1) High THC concentration (10-100mg per piece), (2) Often contain chocolate (double toxicity), (3) Faster absorption from GI tract, (4) Dogs eat multiple pieces quickly. Edibles account for the majority of severe cannabis toxicosis cases in dogs.
ateMarijuana.faqs[3].question: Can a dog die from eating marijuana?
ateMarijuana.faqs[3].answer: Fatalities from marijuana alone are rare in dogs — the LD50 is very high (over 3g/kg of THC). However, edibles pose additional risks: chocolate toxicity, xylitol in some CBD products, and overdose from multiple ingestion. Death is more likely from complications (aspiration pneumonia, hypothermia) or combined toxins. Always seek veterinary care.
ateMarijuana.faqs[4].question: Should I tell my vet my dog ate marijuana?
ateMarijuana.faqs[4].answer: Yes, always be honest. Veterinarians are required to treat, not report, pet poisonings. Knowing your dog ate marijuana ensures they provide appropriate care: inducing vomiting (if early), activated charcoal, IV fluids, thermoregulation, and monitoring heart rate. Without this information, your dog may undergo unnecessary tests or receive inappropriate treatment.

ateXylitolGum.riskAssessment.rows[1].act: 🚨 Emergency vet NOW — liver failure too
ateXylitolGum.steps[0].title: Step 1: Calculate Total Xylitol Consumed
ateXylitolGum.steps[0].content: Find the packaging. Xylitol content is listed in grams per piece. Calculate: grams per piece × pieces eaten. This determines whether hypoglycemia risk (0.1g/kg) or liver failure risk (0.5g/kg) threshold is crossed.
ateXylitolGum.steps[1].title: Step 2: Call Poison Control and Go to Emergency Vet
ateXylitolGum.steps[1].content: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Do NOT wait for symptoms — hypoglycemia can cause death within hours. Xylitol is absorbed rapidly.
ateXylitolGum.steps[2].title: Step 3: Do NOT Induce Vomiting Without Vet Approval
ateXylitolGum.steps[2].content: ⚠️ If instructed to induce at home, use hydrogen peroxide (1 tsp per 5lbs). But go to vet ASAP — xylitol may need IV dextrose to prevent hypoglycemia.
ateXylitolGum.steps[3].title: Step 4: Prepare for Hospitalization
ateXylitolGum.steps[3].content: Your vet will: induce vomiting (if early), give activated charcoal, start IV dextrose, and monitor blood glucose for 24 hours. Liver enzymes will be checked for 72 hours. Early treatment has 80%+ survival.
ateXylitolGum.faqs[0].question: How much xylitol is toxic to dogs?
ateXylitolGum.faqs[0].answer: Xylitol is toxic to dogs at doses as low as 0.1g/kg for hypoglycemia and 0.5g/kg for liver failure. A single piece of sugar-free gum can contain 0.3-1.0g of xylitol — meaning ONE piece can cause severe hypoglycemia in a small-to-medium dog. Emergency treatment is needed even for tiny amounts.
ateXylitolGum.faqs[1].question: What are the symptoms of xylitol poisoning in dogs?
ateXylitolGum.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms appear within 10-60 minutes (sometimes delayed 12 hours): vomiting, lethargy, weakness, collapse, tremors, seizures, and coma — these result from hypoglycemia (low blood sugar). Liver failure symptoms (jaundice, coagulopathy) may be delayed 12-72 hours. Even small amounts cause dangerously low blood sugar.
ateXylitolGum.faqs[2].question: Why is xylitol toxic to dogs but not humans?
ateXylitolGum.faqs[2].answer: In dogs, xylitol is rapidly absorbed and triggers a massive insulin release from the pancreas — 6-7x more than glucose would. This causes profound hypoglycemia. Humans do not have this insulin response. Additionally, xylitol causes dose-dependent hepatocellular necrosis in dogs through mechanisms not seen in humans.
ateXylitolGum.faqs[3].question: What products contain xylitol?
ateXylitolGum.faqs[3].answer: Xylitol is found in: sugar-free gum, mints, peanut butter (some brands), toothpaste, mouthwash, nasal sprays, chewable vitamins, baked goods, ice cream, and "birch sugar" sold as a sweetener. Some brands: Trident, Orbit, Ice Breakers, Eclipse. Always check ingredient lists before giving human food to dogs.
ateXylitolGum.faqs[4].question: Can a dog survive xylitol poisoning?
ateXylitolGum.faqs[4].answer: Yes, with immediate treatment. If caught within 30 minutes, induced vomiting prevents absorption. If hypoglycemia has begun, IV dextrose corrects blood sugar. Even with liver damage, aggressive hospital care (IV fluids, liver protectants, plasma transfusions) has 70-80% survival if treatment begins within 8 hours. Delayed treatment has worse prognosis.

ateChocolate.steps[0].title: Call for Help Immediately
ateChocolate.steps[0].content: Contact ASPCA Animal Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 or your nearest emergency vet. Time is critical — do not wait for symptoms to appear.
ateChocolate.steps[1].title: Gather Information
ateChocolate.steps[1].content: Note the type of chocolate (milk, dark, baking), estimated amount consumed, and your dog's weight. This helps the vet assess toxicity risk.
ateChocolate.steps[2].title: Do NOT Induce Vomiting Without Vet Approval
ateChocolate.steps[2].content: Inducing vomiting can cause aspiration pneumonia or worsen the situation. Only do so if explicitly instructed by a veterinarian.
ateChocolate.steps[3].title: Monitor Symptoms Closely
ateChocolate.steps[3].content: Watch for vomiting, diarrhea, restlessness, increased thirst, rapid breathing, and seizures. Symptoms may appear within 2-4 hours.
ateChocolate.faqs[0].question: How much chocolate is toxic to dogs?
ateChocolate.faqs[0].answer: Toxicity depends on the type of chocolate and your dog's weight. Milk chocolate becomes toxic at approximately 0.5 oz per pound of body weight. Dark chocolate is 2-3x more toxic. Baking chocolate is the most dangerous — as little as 0.1 oz per pound can be lethal. Use our toxicity calculator to assess your dog's specific risk.
ateChocolate.faqs[1].question: How long after eating chocolate will a dog show symptoms?
ateChocolate.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms typically appear within 2-4 hours but can be delayed up to 12 hours. Early signs include vomiting, diarrhea, and restlessness. Severe symptoms (seizures, irregular heartbeat) may appear 6-12 hours after ingestion. Theobromine is absorbed slowly, so symptoms can worsen over time.
ateChocolate.faqs[2].question: Can a dog die from eating chocolate?
ateChocolate.faqs[2].answer: Yes, chocolate can be fatal to dogs. The lethal dose of theobromine is approximately 100-500 mg per kg of body weight. For a 20kg (44lb) dog, this equals roughly 200g of milk chocolate or 100g of dark chocolate. Immediate veterinary treatment significantly improves survival rates.

ateGrapes.steps[0].title: Call Your Vet Immediately
ateGrapes.steps[0].content: Contact your veterinarian or ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 right away. Do not wait for symptoms to appear.
ateGrapes.steps[1].title: Note the Amount
ateGrapes.steps[1].content: Record how many grapes or raisins your dog ate and their weight. This helps determine toxicity risk.
ateGrapes.steps[2].title: Vet May Induce Vomiting
ateGrapes.steps[2].content: If ingestion was recent (within 2 hours), your vet may induce vomiting or administer activated charcoal to prevent absorption.
ateGrapes.steps[3].title: Monitor for 72 Hours
ateGrapes.steps[3].content: Kidney damage may not show symptoms immediately. Watch for vomiting, lethargy, decreased urination, and loss of appetite.
ateGrapes.faqs[0].question: How many grapes are toxic to dogs?
ateGrapes.faqs[0].answer: The toxic dose is not established, but as few as 1-2 grapes can cause kidney failure in some dogs. Raisins are more concentrated and thus more dangerous. There is no known safe amount — any ingestion should be treated as an emergency.
ateGrapes.faqs[1].question: How long after eating grapes do symptoms appear?
ateGrapes.faqs[1].answer: Vomiting and diarrhea typically begin within 6-12 hours. Signs of kidney failure (decreased urination, lethargy, loss of appetite) may not appear until 24-72 hours after ingestion. Early veterinary intervention is critical.
ateGrapes.faqs[2].question: Why are grapes toxic to dogs?
ateGrapes.faqs[2].answer: The exact toxic mechanism is still unknown. Tartaric acid is the suspected toxin, with varying concentrations between grape varieties. This unpredictability makes any grape ingestion potentially dangerous.

ateXylitol.steps[0].title: Call Your Vet NOW
ateXylitol.steps[0].content: Xylitol acts fast. Contact your vet or ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 immediately — do not wait for symptoms.
ateXylitol.steps[1].title: Check the Product Label
ateXylitol.steps[1].content: Find the xylitol content (in grams) and calculate your dog's exposure. Note: it may be listed as 'birch sugar.'
ateXylitol.steps[2].title: Go to the Vet Immediately
ateXylitol.steps[2].content: Your vet will likely induce vomiting (if within 1 hour), start IV dextrose, and monitor liver enzymes for 72 hours.
ateXylitol.steps[3].title: Do NOT Wait for Symptoms
ateXylitol.steps[3].content: By the time symptoms appear (vomiting, lethargy, seizures), treatment may be less effective. Early intervention saves lives.
ateXylitol.faqs[0].question: How much xylitol is toxic to dogs?
ateXylitol.faqs[0].answer: As little as 0.1g of xylitol per kg of body weight can cause hypoglycemia (low blood sugar). Doses above 0.5g/kg can cause acute liver failure. A single piece of sugar-free gum can contain 0.3-1g of xylitol — potentially lethal for a small dog.
ateXylitol.faqs[1].question: How fast does xylitol affect dogs?
ateXylitol.faqs[1].answer: Hypoglycemia can develop within 10-30 minutes of ingestion. Liver damage may take 8-12 hours to manifest. Rapid treatment is essential — do not wait for symptoms.
ateXylitol.faqs[2].question: Where is xylitol found?
ateXylitol.faqs[2].answer: Xylitol is found in sugar-free gum, candy, baked goods, peanut butter, toothpaste, mouthwash, and some medications. Always check labels — it may be listed as 'birch sugar' or 'xylitol'.

ateOnion.steps[0].title: Call Your Vet
ateOnion.steps[0].content: Contact your veterinarian or ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435. Note the amount and type of onion consumed.
ateOnion.steps[1].title: Vet May Induce Vomiting
ateOnion.steps[1].content: If ingestion was recent (within 2 hours), your vet may induce vomiting to prevent further absorption of thiosulfate compounds.
ateOnion.steps[2].title: Monitor for Anemia Symptoms
ateOnion.steps[2].content: Watch for weakness, pale gums, rapid breathing, and reddish-brown urine over the next 1-3 days.
ateOnion.steps[3].title: Blood Work May Be Needed
ateOnion.steps[3].content: Your vet may recommend a CBC blood test to check for Heinz body anemia, which confirms onion toxicity.
ateOnion.faqs[0].question: How much onion is toxic to dogs?
ateOnion.faqs[0].answer: Onion toxicity occurs at approximately 0.5% of the dog's body weight. For a 20kg (44lb) dog, this equals about 100g (3.5oz) of onion. All forms are toxic: raw, cooked, powdered, and dehydrated. Onion powder is especially concentrated and dangerous.
ateOnion.faqs[1].question: How long after eating onion do symptoms appear?
ateOnion.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms typically develop 1-3 days after ingestion as red blood cells are progressively destroyed. Early signs include weakness, pale gums, and reddish urine. Severe cases can lead to collapse and require blood transfusion.
ateOnion.faqs[2].question: Are all onion types toxic to dogs?
ateOnion.faqs[2].answer: Yes — all Allium species are toxic: onions, garlic, leeks, chives, and shallots. Garlic is less toxic per gram but still dangerous in quantity. Cooking does not reduce toxicity. Onion powder is the most concentrated form.

ateSock.steps[0].title: Call Your Vet Immediately
ateSock.steps[0].content: Contact your veterinarian right away. Note when the sock was eaten and your dog's size — this determines urgency.
ateSock.steps[1].title: Do NOT Induce Vomiting
ateSock.steps[1].content: Unlike toxins, foreign objects can cause more damage coming back up. Only induce vomiting if your vet explicitly instructs you to.
ateSock.steps[2].title: Vet May Retrieve Endoscopically
ateSock.steps[2].content: If the sock is still in the stomach (within 12-24 hours), your vet may remove it via endoscopy — a non-surgical procedure using a camera and grabber.
ateSock.steps[3].title: Monitor for Blockage Signs
ateSock.steps[3].content: Watch for vomiting after eating, loss of appetite, abdominal pain, lethargy, and inability to defecate. These require emergency surgery.
ateSock.faqs[0].question: Will my dog pass a sock naturally?
ateSock.faqs[0].answer: Small socks may pass through the digestive tract within 24-48 hours, but this is not guaranteed. Larger socks or those that become lodged can cause life-threatening intestinal blockage. Never wait to see if it passes — consult your vet immediately.
ateSock.faqs[1].question: How long after eating a sock will symptoms appear?
ateSock.faqs[1].answer: Symptoms of intestinal blockage typically appear within 2-24 hours. Watch for vomiting (especially after eating), loss of appetite, abdominal pain, lethargy, and inability to defecate. These are emergency signs.
ateSock.faqs[2].question: What is the treatment for sock ingestion?
ateSock.faqs[2].answer: Treatment depends on location and size. Your vet may induce vomiting (if within 2 hours), perform endoscopy to retrieve the object, or conduct abdominal surgery if the sock has caused a blockage. X-rays and ultrasound help determine the best approach.

ateAntifreeze.steps[0].title: EMERGENCY VET NOW
ateAntifreeze.steps[0].content: Go to the nearest emergency vet immediately. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 en route. Every minute counts.
ateAntifreeze.steps[1].title: Do NOT Wait for Symptoms
ateAntifreeze.steps[1].content: By the time symptoms appear, kidney damage may be irreversible. The antidote must be given within 8-12 hours to be effective.
ateAntifreeze.steps[2].title: Bring the Container
ateAntifreeze.steps[2].content: Take the antifreeze container to the vet. This confirms the active ingredient (ethylene glycol) and concentration.
ateAntifreeze.steps[3].title: Treatment Window is Critical
ateAntifreeze.steps[3].content: Your vet will administer fomepizole (4-MP) or ethanol IV to block metabolism. After 12 hours, treatment is much less effective.
ateAntifreeze.faqs[0].question: How much antifreeze is lethal to dogs?
ateAntifreeze.faqs[0].answer: As little as 1 teaspoon (5ml) of antifreeze can kill a 10lb (4.5kg) dog. The lethal dose of ethylene glycol is approximately 4.4ml per kg of body weight. This makes antifreeze one of the most dangerous household toxins for pets.
ateAntifreeze.faqs[1].question: How fast does antifreeze kill dogs?
ateAntifreeze.faqs[1].answer: Without treatment, antifreeze is fatal within 12-36 hours. The antidote (fomepizole or ethanol) must be administered within 8-12 hours of ingestion to be effective. After kidney failure begins, survival rates drop dramatically.
ateAntifreeze.faqs[2].question: What are the symptoms of antifreeze poisoning?
ateAntifreeze.faqs[2].answer: Stage 1 (30 min-12 hrs): drunken behavior, vomiting, seizures. Stage 2 (12-24 hrs): apparent improvement (misleading). Stage 3 (24-72 hrs): kidney failure, severe lethargy, mouth ulcers, coma. Early treatment is critical.
